final_note: You worked through C4.1 Populations and communities — 18 guide statements.

concepts.def: An interacting group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time. Members of a population normally breed with one another, so a population is a reproductive unit as well as an ecological one.

The absence of interbreeding between two groups of the same species, usually because they are separated by a geographical barrier or distance. Reproductive isolation is used to distinguish one population of a species from another: individuals in separate populations could interbreed if brought together, but in practice do not.

A sampling procedure in which every part of the area, or every individual, has an equal chance of being selected, for example by placing quadrats at coordinates generated from random numbers. Randomness removes bias due to the investigator's choices, so that the sample is representative of the whole population.

The difference between an estimate of population size obtained from a random sample and the true size of the whole population. Sampling error is an inevitable consequence of measuring a sample rather than the entire population; it is reduced, but not eliminated, by taking larger samples.

A value for the number of individuals in a population calculated from data collected in a sample, rather than by counting every individual. Estimation is used because counting entire populations is usually impractical: it takes too long, may damage the habitat or disturb the organisms, and some individuals are hidden or mobile.

A square frame of known area placed on the ground, or on a rocky shore, within which the individuals of a species are counted. Quadrats are placed at random positions, and the mean number of individuals per quadrat is scaled up by the total area to estimate population size.

An organism that does not move from place to place, such as a plant, a lichen, or an animal such as a barnacle, a mussel or a sea anemone that is fixed to a surface. Random quadrat sampling is suitable for sessile organisms because they do not move into or out of the quadrat while it is being counted.

concepts.term: Standard deviation of the mean number per quadrat
concepts.def: A measure of how widely the individual quadrat counts are spread around their mean, obtained with a calculator. A small standard deviation shows that most quadrats contain similar numbers of individuals, so the population is spread evenly; a large standard deviation shows that counts vary greatly between quadrats, so the population is clumped or patchy.

A method of estimating the population size of motile organisms. A sample of individuals is captured, marked in a harmless way and released. After the marked individuals have mixed back into the population, a second sample is captured and the number of marked individuals in it is recorded.

The calculation used to estimate population size from capture–mark–release–recapture data: population size estimate = M × N / R, where M is the number of individuals caught and marked initially, N is the total number of individuals recaptured and R is the number of marked individuals recaptured. It rests on the proportion of marked individuals in the second sample being the same as the proportion in the whole population.

The conditions that must hold for the estimate to be reliable: marked individuals mix randomly back into the population before recapture; marks are not lost and do not change the chance of an individual surviving or being recaptured; and there are no births, deaths, immigration or emigration between the two sampling occasions.

The maximum population size of a species that a particular environment can support sustainably. It is set by the availability of limited resources such as food, water, light, space, mineral nutrients or nesting sites, and it can change if the supply of those resources changes.

A resource that is in short supply relative to the needs of a population and so restricts its growth. Individuals compete for limiting resources; for plants these are often light, water, space and mineral ions, and for animals food, water, territory, mates and nesting or shelter sites.

A factor whose effect on the proportion of individuals surviving or reproducing becomes stronger as the population becomes more dense. Examples are competition for limited resources, the increased risk of predation, and the more rapid transfer of pathogens or pests between individuals in a dense population.

A factor that affects the same proportion of a population regardless of its density, such as an extreme weather event, a flood, a fire or a volcanic eruption. Density-independent factors cause population numbers to fluctuate but do not push the population back towards its carrying capacity.

concepts.term: Negative feedback control of population size
concepts.def: The tendency of density-dependent factors to return a population towards its carrying capacity. When numbers rise above the carrying capacity, competition, predation and disease increase, so mortality rises and natality falls; when numbers fall below it, these pressures ease, so the population grows again.

Population growth in which the number of individuals increases by a constant proportion in each unit of time, so the population doubles at regular intervals. It occurs in the initial phase of growth because resources are plentiful and competition, predation and disease are negligible, so natality exceeds mortality and the number of reproducing individuals rises each generation.

An idealized graphical model of population growth in which an exponential phase is followed by a transitional phase of slowing growth and then a plateau at the carrying capacity. Because it is a simplification of a complex system, real populations often fluctuate around or overshoot the plateau rather than following the curve exactly.

The phase of the sigmoid growth curve in which the population size stays roughly constant at the carrying capacity. Births and deaths continue, but natality and mortality are equal because density-dependent factors have become intense enough to balance reproduction.

concepts.term: Logarithmic scale test for exponential growth
concepts.def: A graph of population size on a logarithmic vertical axis against time on a non-logarithmic horizontal axis. If growth is exponential, the population increases by the same factor in each time interval, which appears as a straight line on this graph; a line that bends downwards shows that growth has slowed below exponential.

concepts.term: Reindeer of St Paul Island (case study)
concepts.def: A real case of population growth in an ecosystem: 25 reindeer introduced to St Paul Island, Alaska, in 1911 grew to about 2000 by 1938 with almost no predation, then collapsed to a few individuals in the 1950s after overgrazing of the lichens that were their winter food. The growth resembled the exponential phase of the model but the population overshot the carrying capacity and crashed instead of levelling off.

A population of an organism that proliferates under laboratory conditions, such as yeast in a sugar solution or duckweed on the surface of a container of water, used to collect data on population growth over time. Sampling and counting at intervals produces a growth curve that can be compared with the sigmoid model.

Competition between members of the same population for a resource that is in limited supply. It arises because individuals of one species have the same requirements, so they need exactly the same resources; examples are trees in a stand competing for light, and male red deer competing for mates.

Behaviour in which members of the same population act together in ways that benefit each of them, such as wolves hunting in a pack, meerkats taking turns as sentinels to warn of predators, and honeybee workers foraging and defending a shared colony. Cooperation and competition can both occur within the same population.

All of the interacting organisms living in an ecosystem: every population in the area, including the plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. A community includes only the living components; together with the abiotic environment it forms the ecosystem.
An interspecific relationship in which an animal feeds on a plant or alga, for example a caterpillar eating leaves or a limpet grazing algae from rock. The plant is usually damaged but not killed.
An interspecific relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another animal, the prey, for example a lynx killing a snowshoe hare.

An interspecific relationship in which two species require the same limited resource, so the use of it by one reduces its availability to the other; for example, grey and red squirrels competing for acorns. The species need not meet or fight for competition to occur.

An interspecific relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another organism, the host, obtaining nutrition from it and harming it but not usually killing it directly; for example a tick feeding on the blood of a deer, or a tapeworm in the intestine of a mammal.

An interspecific relationship in which a microorganism or virus lives in a host and causes disease in it, for example the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis causing tuberculosis in humans, or Phytophthora infestans causing potato blight.

An interspecific relationship in which both species benefit. Each partner supplies the other with something it cannot obtain, or cannot obtain as easily, on its own, so both grow or reproduce better together than apart.

Swellings on the roots of legumes (Fabaceae) such as peas, beans and clover that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium). The bacteria convert nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia and then amino acids that the plant uses; the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars from photosynthesis and a protected environment inside the nodule.

A mutualism between an orchid and a fungus whose hyphae grow into the orchid's roots. Orchid seeds are tiny and have almost no food reserves, so the germinating seedling depends on the fungus for carbon compounds as well as mineral ions and water absorbed from the soil; once the orchid photosynthesizes it supplies the fungus with sugars.

A mutualism between reef-building coral polyps and photosynthetic single-celled algae (zooxanthellae) that live inside the polyp's cells. The algae supply the coral with carbon compounds such as sugars and with oxygen from photosynthesis; the coral provides the algae with a protected position in shallow sunlit water, carbon dioxide and nitrogen-containing waste such as ammonium.

A species that occurs naturally in a particular area, having evolved or arrived there without human introduction. In the guide's usage (C4.1.13) 'endemic' is contrasted with 'introduced', so a native species such as the red squirrel in Britain counts as endemic even if it also lives elsewhere. Endemic species are often outcompeted for resources by introduced species that have a competitive advantage.

An introduced species that spreads and increases in an area outside its natural range, harming endemic species. The grey squirrel, introduced to Britain from North America, has largely replaced the endemic red squirrel: it is larger, stores more fat, can digest unripe acorns that red squirrels cannot, and so gains more of the shared food supply.

A test for interspecific competition in which the investigator removes one species from some plots in the field and leaves other plots untouched, then compares the success of the remaining species. Greater success where the other species has been removed indicates, but does not prove, that the two species compete.

Two ways of testing a hypothesis. In an experiment the investigator deliberately changes a variable, for example by removing a species or growing two species together in the laboratory, and records the effect. In an observation, such as random sampling of where two species occur in the field, the investigator records what is already there without altering it. Both can test hypotheses, but only an experiment manipulates the conditions.

A statistical test applied to presence/absence data for two species recorded in many sampling sites. The null hypothesis is that the two species are distributed independently; observed frequencies are compared with the frequencies expected if there were no association, and a chi-squared value greater than the critical value (3.84 at p = 0.05 with one degree of freedom) means the association is significant.

concepts.term: Expected frequency in a contingency table
concepts.def: The number of sites in a category that would be expected if the two species were distributed independently, calculated as (row total × column total) / grand total. If both species are present together in fewer sites than expected the association is negative, which may provide evidence of interspecific competition.

A real case study of density-dependent control: fur records of the Hudson's Bay Company show that numbers of snowshoe hares and Canada lynx in northern Canada rose and fell in cycles of roughly 10 years, with each peak in lynx numbers following the peak in hares. More hares allow more lynx to survive and breed; more lynx then reduce hare numbers, after which lynx numbers fall and hares recover.

Control of population sizes in a community by the organisms at higher trophic levels. Predators or herbivores limit the populations they feed on, and the effect passes down the food chain: for example, where sea otters are abundant they keep sea urchin numbers low, which allows kelp to flourish.

Control of population sizes in a community by the supply of resources at the base of the food chain. The availability of light, water or mineral nutrients limits producers, which in turn limits the herbivores and then the predators that depend on them; for example, low nitrate and phosphate supply limits phytoplankton and so the zooplankton and fish that feed on them.

The release by a plant of a chemical substance into the environment that inhibits the germination or growth of potential competitors. For example, black walnut (Juglans nigra) releases juglone from its roots and fallen leaves, which suppresses many other plants growing beneath it.

The release by a microorganism of a chemical substance that inhibits or kills competing microorganisms in its environment. For example, the mould Penicillium secretes penicillin, which prevents bacteria from growing on the same food source. Like allelopathy, this deters potential competitors by releasing a chemical into the environment.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a population is correct?
options: Its members belong to one species, live in the same area and normally breed with one another.
It includes every member of a species, wherever in the world that species is found.
It includes all the organisms of every species that interact within one area.
Its members cannot interbreed with members of other populations of the species.
mcqs.specStatementText: A population is one species, one area, interbreeding
mcqs.explain: A population is an interacting group of organisms of the same species living in an area, and its members normally breed with each other. Reproductive isolation is what distinguishes one population of a species from another.
rationales: A population is an interacting group of organisms of the same species living in an area, and its members normally breed with each other. Reproductive isolation is what distinguishes one population of a species from another.
A student who uses the everyday sense of 'the elephant population' picks this. In fact a population is tied to an area; a species usually consists of many separate populations.
A student who transfers the idea of a town's population to a habitat picks this. In fact that describes a community; a population contains only one species.

A student who reads reproductive isolation as biological incompatibility picks this. In fact members of separate populations remain one species and could interbreed if brought together; they simply do not, being separated.

mcqs.q: Two groups of great crested newts breed in ponds 5 km apart, and no newt ever moves between the ponds. How should the two groups be described?
options: Two species, because groups that do not interbreed cannot belong to the same species.
Two populations of one species, because the groups are reproductively isolated from each other.
One population, because all the newts belong to the same species, wherever they breed.
Two communities, because each pond contains newts together with the other organisms living in it.
mcqs.specStatementText: A population is one species, one area, interbreeding
mcqs.explain: The newts are the same species, but because no individual moves between the ponds the two groups never interbreed. Reproductive isolation of this kind is used to distinguish one population from another.
rationales: A student who equates reproductive isolation between populations with the isolation that separates species picks this. In fact the newts could interbreed if brought together; they are one species in two populations.

The newts are the same species, but because no individual moves between the ponds the two groups never interbreed. Reproductive isolation of this kind is used to distinguish one population from another.
A student who thinks a population is the whole species picks this. In fact a population is an interacting group in one area whose members normally breed together, which these two groups never do.
A student who merges 'population' with 'all the organisms in a place' picks this. In fact the question concerns the newts alone, one species, so the groups are populations, not communities.

mcqs.q: Why do ecologists usually estimate the size of a population rather than counting every individual?
options: A large enough random sample gives the true population size exactly, so a complete count is unnecessary.
Sampling lets the investigator select the most typical parts of the habitat in which to count.
Counting every individual is usually impractical and may damage the habitat or disturb the organisms.
The number counted in the sample quadrats is itself the population size, so no further counting is needed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
mcqs.explain: Complete counts take too long over large areas, individuals may be hidden or mobile, and searching the whole habitat can damage it. A random sample gives a usable estimate at far lower cost.
rationales: A student who believes that good technique removes all error picks this. In fact any estimate from a sample carries a sampling error; estimation is a practical compromise, not a way of obtaining the exact size.

A student who thinks choosing representative sites is the point of sampling picks this. In fact sampling sites must be chosen at random, precisely to remove the investigator's choice and the bias it introduces.
Complete counts take too long over large areas, individuals may be hidden or mobile, and searching the whole habitat can damage it. A random sample gives a usable estimate at far lower cost.
A student who treats the sample count as the result picks this. In fact the sample count is scaled up by the total area to give the estimate; it is not the population size.

mcqs.q: A student uses random quadrats to estimate that a rocky shore holds 420 limpets. A later complete count finds 460. Which statement about the sampling error is correct?
options: It is 40 limpets, and arose from mistakes the student made when counting inside the quadrats.
It would have been zero if the student had placed enough quadrats to sample the shore properly.
It arose because the quadrats were placed at random instead of in areas typical of the whole shore.
It is 40 limpets, and arose because only a sample of the shore was measured, not all of it.
mcqs.specStatementText: Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
mcqs.explain: Sampling error is the difference between the estimate (420) and the true size (460), which is 40. It is the inevitable consequence of measuring a random sample rather than the whole population.
rationales: A student who thinks 'error' means a blunder picks this. In fact sampling error occurs even with perfect counting, because a random sample can by chance contain a lower or higher density than the shore as a whole.

A student who thinks enough quadrats guarantee the true value picks this. In fact more quadrats reduce the sampling error on average but cannot eliminate it; only a complete count has no sampling error.

A student who prefers chosen 'typical' sites to random ones picks this. In fact random placement is what makes the estimate unbiased; choosing sites would add bias on top of the unavoidable sampling error.
Sampling error is the difference between the estimate (420) and the true size (460), which is 40. It is the inevitable consequence of measuring a random sample rather than the whole population.

mcqs.q: A student places ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in a 250 m² meadow and counts 20 orchids in total. What is the estimated population of orchids in the meadow?
options: 2000 plants
20 plants
500 plants
20000 plants
mcqs.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
mcqs.explain: Each quadrat is 0.25 m², so the sampled area is 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 m². Density = 20 ÷ 2.5 = 8 orchids per m², and 8 × 250 m² = 2000 orchids.
rationales: Each quadrat is 0.25 m², so the sampled area is 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 m². Density = 20 ÷ 2.5 = 8 orchids per m², and 8 × 250 m² = 2000 orchids.
A student who takes the sample count as the population picks this. In fact the 20 orchids were counted in only 2.5 m² of a 250 m² meadow and must be scaled up by the total area.
A student who treats each quadrat as 1 m² picks this: a mean of 2 per quadrat × 250 m². In fact a 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat is 0.25 m², so the density is 8 per m², not 2.
A student who divides the total count by the area of a single quadrat (20 ÷ 0.25 = 80 per m²) picks this. In fact the 20 orchids came from ten quadrats, a sampled area of 2.5 m², giving 8 per m².

mcqs.q: Limpets were counted in twenty random quadrats on each of two shores. On both shores the mean was 8 limpets per quadrat. The standard deviation was 1.2 on shore A and 6.5 on shore B. What can be concluded?
options: Shore B has a larger limpet population than shore A, because its standard deviation is higher.
Limpets on shore B are distributed less evenly, because the counts varied much more from quadrat to quadrat.
The sampling on shore B was carried out incorrectly, so its mean of 8 per quadrat is not valid.
Using more quadrats on shore B would have reduced its standard deviation to about that of shore A.
mcqs.specStatementText: Quadrats for things that stay put
mcqs.explain: The standard deviation of the mean number per quadrat measures variation between quadrat counts and so shows how evenly the population is spread. A larger standard deviation with the same mean means a patchier, more clumped distribution.
rationales: A student who reads any larger statistic as 'more limpets' picks this. In fact population size is estimated from the mean, which is the same on both shores; the standard deviation describes spread, not number.

The standard deviation of the mean number per quadrat measures variation between quadrat counts and so shows how evenly the population is spread. A larger standard deviation with the same mean means a patchier, more clumped distribution.

A student who treats a large deviation as a sign of faulty work picks this. In fact a clumped population produces a large standard deviation however carefully the sampling is done; it is information about the shore, not the student.

A student who thinks larger samples remove variation picks this. In fact the standard deviation reflects the real unevenness of the limpets on shore B; more quadrats would estimate that spread more precisely, not shrink it.

mcqs.q: In a capture–mark–release–recapture study, 40 woodlice were caught, marked and released. Later, 50 woodlice were caught, of which 10 were marked. What is the Lincoln index estimate of the population?
options: About 8
About 2000
About 200
About 80
mcqs.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
mcqs.explain: Population estimate = M × N ÷ R = 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200. One fifth of the second sample was marked, so the 40 marked woodlice are estimated to be one fifth of the population.
rationales: A student who does not see that the estimate rests on the proportion marked, and so places R in the numerator (M × R ÷ N = 40 × 10 ÷ 50), picks this. In fact the estimate cannot be smaller than the 40 woodlice already marked; R is the denominator.

A student who thinks the two sample sizes alone give the estimate multiplies M by N and forgets to divide by R. In fact the proportion of marked woodlice recaptured (10 of 50) must be used to scale M up, giving 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200.
Population estimate = M × N ÷ R = 40 × 50 ÷ 10 = 200. One fifth of the second sample was marked, so the 40 marked woodlice are estimated to be one fifth of the population.
A student who adds up the distinct woodlice seen (40 marked plus 40 unmarked in the second sample) picks this. In fact the method estimates the individuals never caught; M × N ÷ R gives 200.

mcqs.q: Beetles were marked with a spot of bright paint that made them easier for birds to see. Compared with the true population size, what will the Lincoln index estimate be, and why?
options: Too low, because fewer marked beetles are recaptured and fewer recaptures mean a smaller population.
Unaffected, provided the second sample is taken at the release point soon after the beetles are released.
Too low, because fewer beetles in total are encountered across the two samples, so fewer are counted.
Too high, because fewer marked beetles survive to be recaptured, so R is too small.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mark, release, recapture for things that move
mcqs.explain: The method assumes marking does not affect survival. Marked beetles are eaten preferentially, so the marked fraction in the second sample is lower than it should be; with R smaller, M × N ÷ R is larger than the true population.
rationales: A student who reasons by direct proportion picks this. In fact R is the denominator of M × N ÷ R, so a smaller R makes the estimate larger, not smaller.

A student who thinks the aim is to recapture as many marked beetles as possible picks this. In fact sampling before the marked beetles mix in breaks a different assumption of the method, and does not cancel the effect of predation on marked beetles.
A student who thinks the estimate is the number of beetles seen picks this. In fact the estimate depends on the proportion marked in the second sample, and a reduced proportion inflates the estimate.

The method assumes marking does not affect survival. Marked beetles are eaten preferentially, so the marked fraction in the second sample is lower than it should be; with R smaller, M × N ÷ R is larger than the true population.

mcqs.q: Which statement gives the meaning of the carrying capacity of an environment for a species?
options: The maximum population size that the resources available in the environment can support sustainably over time.
The number of individuals that can physically fit into the area that the population occupies.
The greatest number of offspring that each individual of the species is able to produce in its lifetime.
The population size below which negative feedback stops reducing the numbers of a species in its environment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Carrying capacity is set by limited resources
mcqs.explain: Carrying capacity is set by the supply of limiting resources such as food, water, light, space, mineral nutrients or nesting sites; it is the largest population the environment can maintain over time.
rationales: Carrying capacity is set by the supply of limiting resources such as food, water, light, space, mineral nutrients or nesting sites; it is the largest population the environment can maintain over time.
A student who uses 'capacity' in the sense of a bus or a stadium picks this. In fact resources, not room, set the limit, and populations stop growing long before the area is physically full.

A student who thinks carrying capacity is a fixed property of the species picks this. In fact it belongs to the environment: the same species has different carrying capacities in habitats with different resource supplies.

A student who reads negative feedback as a one-way downward pressure picks this. In fact carrying capacity is the size the environment's resources can sustain, and density-dependent feedback acts in both directions around it: pushing numbers down when above it and allowing growth when below it.

mcqs.q: A storm kills 30% of a seabird colony. Over the following years, the colony returns to its former size. Which explanation is correct?
options: The storm was a density-dependent factor, because it killed so many birds in a colony as large as this one was.
The storm was density-independent; reduced competition afterwards let natality exceed mortality until carrying capacity was regained.
Density-dependent factors can only ever reduce populations, so the recovery afterwards must have been due to density-independent factors.
The recovery shows that the carrying capacity is fixed by the birds' breeding rate rather than by the environment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
mcqs.explain: A storm kills a similar proportion of birds whatever the colony's density, so it is density-independent. Once numbers fell, density-dependent pressures such as competition for food and nest sites relaxed, and negative feedback returned the population towards the carrying capacity.
rationales: A student who judges by the number killed rather than the proportion picks this. In fact a storm kills roughly the same fraction of a small or a large colony, which makes it density-independent.

A storm kills a similar proportion of birds whatever the colony's density, so it is density-independent. Once numbers fell, density-dependent pressures such as competition for food and nest sites relaxed, and negative feedback returned the population towards the carrying capacity.
A student who sees density-dependent factors purely as brakes picks this. In fact their effect weakens at low density, and that relaxation is exactly what allows the population to grow back.

A student who thinks carrying capacity is a property of the species picks this. In fact the colony returned to the size that the local food and nesting resources can support, which is what carrying capacity means.

mcqs.q: Which statement about density-dependent factors is correct?
options: Any factor that kills more individuals when the population is larger, including a flood or a frost, is density-dependent.
Predation and disease are density-independent, since predators and pathogens come from outside the population.
The proportion of individuals they kill or prevent from breeding rises as the population becomes more dense.
They act as negative feedback, so they continue to reduce the population until it is very small.
mcqs.specStatementText: Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
mcqs.explain: Density-dependent factors, which include competition for limited resources, the increased risk of predation and the transfer of pathogens or pests, affect a larger fraction of the population at higher density, so they push numbers back towards the carrying capacity.
rationales: A student who counts deaths instead of comparing proportions picks this. In fact a flood affects a similar fraction at any density; it is density-independent even though more individuals die in a larger population.

A student who limits density dependence to competition picks this. In fact dense populations suffer a higher risk of predation and faster transfer of pathogens or pests, so both are density-dependent.

Density-dependent factors, which include competition for limited resources, the increased risk of predation and the transfer of pathogens or pests, affect a larger fraction of the population at higher density, so they push numbers back towards the carrying capacity.

A student who reads 'negative' as 'downward' picks this. In fact negative feedback opposes change in either direction: the same factors that reduce a large population relax and allow a small one to recover.

mcqs.q: Why is the growth of a population exponential in its initial phase?
options: Each individual reproduces faster and faster as the phase continues.
Individuals reach maturity sooner than they will later at higher density.
Growth continues at full speed until the food has been entirely used up.
Resources are plentiful, so most individuals survive to reproduce.
mcqs.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
mcqs.explain: With abundant resources and negligible competition, predation and disease, natality exceeds mortality by a roughly constant proportion. Each generation adds to the number of reproducing individuals, so the population increases by a constant factor per unit time.
rationales: A student who confuses the population's growth rate with the per-individual rate picks this. In fact each individual's reproductive rate stays roughly constant; the population accelerates because more individuals are reproducing.

A student who explains acceleration by faster individual development picks this. In fact the explanation is a constant proportional increase applied to a growing number of individuals, not a change in each one.
A student who thinks food acts as a switch picks this. In fact growth slows through a transitional phase as resources become scarcer per individual, well before any resource is exhausted.

With abundant resources and negligible competition, predation and disease, natality exceeds mortality by a roughly constant proportion. Each generation adds to the number of reproducing individuals, so the population increases by a constant factor per unit time.

mcqs.q: A student records the size of a duckweed population every two days and plots it on a logarithmic vertical axis against time on a non-logarithmic horizontal axis. Which observation would show that growth was exponential?
options: The points lie on a straight line, because the population multiplied by the same factor in each two-day interval.
The points form a curve that becomes steeper with time, as exponential growth does on ordinary axes.
The points lie on a straight line, because a fixed number of plants was added in each two-day interval.
The points trace an S-shaped curve, because all populations grow according to the sigmoid model.
mcqs.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
mcqs.explain: On a logarithmic axis, equal multiples occupy equal distances. Exponential growth multiplies the population by a constant factor per interval, so it appears as a straight line; a line that bends downwards would show growth slowing.
rationales: On a logarithmic axis, equal multiples occupy equal distances. Exponential growth multiplies the population by a constant factor per interval, so it appears as a straight line; a line that bends downwards would show growth slowing.

A student who treats the J-shape as the definition of exponential growth picks this. In fact the logarithmic axis straightens a J-curve; a curve still steepening on a log scale would mean growth faster than exponential.

A student who thinks exponential growth means a constant number added per interval picks this. In fact that would be linear growth, which is straight on ordinary axes but bends over on a logarithmic axis.

A student who mistakes the model for reality picks this. In fact the sigmoid curve is an idealized model; on this graph the test for exponential growth is a straight line, and an S-shape would show that growth had slowed and stopped.

mcqs.q: In 1911, 25 reindeer were introduced to St Paul Island, Alaska, where they had almost no predators. By 1938 there were about 2000; by 1950 only 8 remained, after the lichens they ate in winter had been destroyed. How should this be interpreted in relation to the sigmoid growth model?
options: The reindeer must have levelled off at a plateau at some point between 1938 and 1950 that the counts simply failed to record properly.
The model is a simplification: the reindeer overshot the carrying capacity because their food was destroyed faster than it regrew.
The crash shows that the carrying capacity of reindeer is fixed at about 2000 animals, wherever they live.
Negative feedback pushed the population down and would continue to reduce it until the reindeer were extinct.
mcqs.specStatementText: The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
mcqs.explain: The sigmoid curve is an idealized model in which growth slows smoothly to a plateau. Real populations can grow past the carrying capacity if the limiting resource is depleted faster than the feedback acts; the lichen was destroyed, the carrying capacity fell, and the population crashed.
rationales: A student who believes the model must be obeyed picks this. In fact the data are the evidence, and they show an overshoot and crash; the model, not the data, is the simplification.

The sigmoid curve is an idealized model in which growth slows smoothly to a plateau. Real populations can grow past the carrying capacity if the limiting resource is depleted faster than the feedback acts; the lichen was destroyed, the carrying capacity fell, and the population crashed.

A student who treats carrying capacity as a species constant picks this. In fact carrying capacity belongs to the environment; on this island it was set by the lichen supply, and it fell when the lichen was destroyed.

A student who reads negative feedback as a one-way decline picks this. In fact negative feedback returns a population towards the carrying capacity; the crash reflected a collapse in the carrying capacity itself.

mcqs.q: Yeast was grown in a sealed flask of glucose solution and cell counts were made every four hours. After 24 hours the count stopped rising. Which explanation for the plateau is correct?
options: The yeast cells have all stopped dividing, and none of them are dying, so the count stays the same.
The plateau is reached only at the moment when the glucose in the flask has been completely used up.
Natality now equals mortality, because glucose has become scarce and ethanol has accumulated.
The flask has reached the carrying capacity that applies to yeast in any environment.
mcqs.specStatementText: Growing a population in the lab
mcqs.explain: In a closed culture, density-dependent factors intensify as the population grows: glucose per cell falls, ethanol and other wastes build up and pH falls. Cell division slows and death rises until the two balance at the carrying capacity of the flask.
rationales: A student who reads a flat line as inactivity picks this. In fact cells continue to divide and to die during the plateau; the count is constant because the two rates are equal.

A student who treats food as the only limit and as a switch picks this. In fact growth slows progressively as glucose becomes scarcer, and the accumulation of ethanol limits the population at the same time.

In a closed culture, density-dependent factors intensify as the population grows: glucose per cell falls, ethanol and other wastes build up and pH falls. Cell division slows and death rises until the two balance at the carrying capacity of the flask.

A student who thinks carrying capacity is a fixed property of yeast picks this. In fact the plateau is set by the resources and waste levels in this flask; a larger flask or more glucose would give a higher plateau.

mcqs.q: Which pair gives one example of intraspecific competition followed by one example of intraspecific cooperation?
options: Grey squirrels taking acorns from red squirrels; wolves hunting together as a pack.
Sardines swimming together in a shoal; emperor penguins huddling against the cold.
Lions and hyenas fighting over a carcass; ants guarding aphids in return for honeydew.
Oak seedlings shading each other; meerkats taking turns as sentinels.
mcqs.specStatementText: Same species: compete and cooperate
mcqs.explain: Seedlings of one species in a dense stand compete for light because they have identical needs. Meerkat sentinels give a warning that benefits every member of the group, at a cost to the sentinel's own foraging time, which is cooperation within a species.
rationales: A student who thinks competition only happens between species picks this. In fact grey and red squirrels are different species, so that is interspecific competition; pack hunting is a correct example of cooperation.
A student who reads any grouping as the whole story picks this. In fact both examples are cooperation; neither is intraspecific competition, so the pair does not match the question.

A student who treats all the animals in an area as one population picks this. In fact both examples involve two different species: an interspecific competition and a mutualism, not relationships within a species.

Seedlings of one species in a dense stand compete for light because they have identical needs. Meerkat sentinels give a warning that benefits every member of the group, at a cost to the sentinel's own foraging time, which is cooperation within a species.

mcqs.q: Which description of a community is correct?
options: All the populations of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria that live and interact in an area.
All the populations of plants and animals, but not microorganisms, that live in an area.
All the organisms in an area together with the soil, water and climate they depend on.
All the individuals of one species that live, interact and breed together in an area.
mcqs.specStatementText: A community is all the living things in an ecosystem
mcqs.explain: A community is all of the interacting organisms in an ecosystem: every population in the area, including the plants, animals, fungi and bacteria, but not the abiotic environment.
rationales: A community is all of the interacting organisms in an ecosystem: every population in the area, including the plants, animals, fungi and bacteria, but not the abiotic environment.
A student whose mental picture comes from food-web diagrams picks this. In fact fungi and bacteria are populations too and are part of the community as decomposers, pathogens and mutualists.
A student who attaches the abiotic environment to the wrong term picks this. In fact this describes an ecosystem; the community is the living part only.
A student who has not separated 'population' from 'community' picks this. In fact this is the definition of a population; a community contains all the populations of every species in the area.

mcqs.q: A tick attaches to a deer and feeds on its blood for several days before dropping off. Which category of interspecific relationship is this?
options: Predation, because the tick is an animal feeding on the body of another animal.
Parasitism, because the tick takes nutrition from a living host without killing it.
Pathogenicity, because the tick is a small organism that harms a much larger one.
Mutualism, because the deer provides the tick with the food that it needs to survive.
mcqs.specStatementText: Six ways species interact
mcqs.explain: A parasite lives on or in its host, obtains food from it over a period of time and harms it, but does not usually kill it. The tick feeding on the deer's blood fits this exactly.
rationales: A student who calls any animal that feeds on another a predator picks this. In fact a predator kills its prey and eats it; the deer survives the tick, so the relationship is parasitism.
A parasite lives on or in its host, obtains food from it over a period of time and harms it, but does not usually kill it. The tick feeding on the deer's blood fits this exactly.
A student who stretches 'pathogen' to mean anything harmful picks this. In fact pathogenicity is disease caused by a microorganism or virus living in a host; the tick is a parasite taking food.
A student who thinks mutualism means one species providing for another picks this. In fact mutualism requires both species to benefit, and the deer gains nothing from losing blood to the tick.

mcqs.q: What are the benefits to each partner in the relationship between a legume and the bacteria in its root nodules?
options: The bacteria supply the plant with nitrogen gas from the soil; the plant supplies the bacteria with oxygen.
The plant gains fixed nitrogen from the bacteria; the bacteria gain nothing from the plant but are not harmed by living in the nodule.
The bacteria supply the plant with fixed nitrogen as ammonia or amino acids; the plant supplies the bacteria with sugars.
The bacteria take sugars from the roots and give the plant nothing, so the nodules are a mild infection the plant tolerates.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
mcqs.explain: Rhizobium bacteria in the nodules of Fabaceae convert nitrogen gas into ammonia, which the plant uses to make amino acids. In return the plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis and a protected environment inside the nodule, so both benefit.
rationales: A student who uses 'nitrogen' loosely picks this. In fact plants cannot use nitrogen gas at all; the whole point of the relationship is that the bacteria fix the gas into ammonia the plant can use.
A student who remembers only the plant's side picks this. In fact mutualism means both partners benefit: the bacteria receive sugars made by photosynthesis and a sheltered environment.

Rhizobium bacteria in the nodules of Fabaceae convert nitrogen gas into ammonia, which the plant uses to make amino acids. In return the plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis and a protected environment inside the nodule, so both benefit.

A student who assumes microorganisms inside roots must be harmful picks this. In fact legumes with nodules grow better in nitrogen-poor soil than legumes without them, because they receive fixed nitrogen.

mcqs.q: When sea temperatures rise, hard corals expel their zooxanthellae, turn white and often die of starvation within weeks. Why does losing the algae starve the coral?
options: The coral can no longer photosynthesize, because the algae carried its chlorophyll for it.
The coral loses the shelter and the carbon dioxide that the algae had been providing for it.
The algae were parasites, so the coral is weakened by the damage they caused before being expelled.
The coral loses the sugars and other carbon compounds the algae made by photosynthesis.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
mcqs.explain: Zooxanthellae living inside the polyp's cells photosynthesize and pass most of the carbon compounds they make to the coral, along with oxygen. Without them the coral polyp, an animal, cannot obtain enough food from the plankton it catches.
rationales: A student who thinks the coral is itself photosynthetic picks this. In fact the coral polyp is an animal and has no chlorophyll of its own; photosynthesis is done entirely by the zooxanthellae.

A student who has the direction of the benefits reversed picks this. In fact the coral provides the algae with shelter, a sunlit position and carbon dioxide; the algae provide the coral with carbon compounds and oxygen.

A student who assumes an organism living inside another must be harming it picks this. In fact the relationship is mutualism: the coral starves after the expulsion because it has lost a partner, not because of earlier damage.

Zooxanthellae living inside the polyp's cells photosynthesize and pass most of the carbon compounds they make to the coral, along with oxygen. Without them the coral polyp, an animal, cannot obtain enough food from the plankton it catches.

mcqs.q: The grey squirrel was introduced to Britain from North America in the nineteenth century and has replaced the endemic red squirrel across most of England and Wales. Which statement correctly describes the competitive advantage in resource acquisition that underlies this invasion?
options: Grey squirrels digest unripe acorns and store more fat, so they take a larger share of the shared food supply and out-reproduce red squirrels.
Grey squirrels kill red squirrels and their young in fights, so red squirrels are driven out of any wood the greys enter.
Red squirrels, being adapted to British woodland, hold their ground wherever food is scarce, so greys spread only where food is plentiful.
The two species compete only where individuals meet and fight over the same acorn, so replacement happens only in crowded woods.
mcqs.specStatementText: Invasive species win the competition for resources
mcqs.explain: The basis of an introduced species becoming invasive is a competitive advantage in acquiring resources. Grey squirrels are larger, can eat acorns before they ripen and survive winter better, so where the two species share a wood the red squirrel population declines.
rationales: The basis of an introduced species becoming invasive is a competitive advantage in acquiring resources. Grey squirrels are larger, can eat acorns before they ripen and survive winter better, so where the two species share a wood the red squirrel population declines.

A student who pictures invasion as aggression picks this. In fact grey squirrels do not need to attack red squirrels; taking more of the shared food is enough to reduce red squirrel survival and breeding.

A student who assumes the endemic species must be better fitted to its habitat picks this. In fact the red squirrel is adapted to its former competitors, not to the grey squirrel, and loses out where food is limited.
A student who thinks competition requires a direct contest picks this. In fact competition occurs whenever both species draw on the same limited resource, whether or not individuals ever meet.

mcqs.q: On a rocky shore, barnacle species A is found on the lower shore only where barnacle species B is absent. When B is scraped from some plots on the lower shore, A colonises them and grows well. What can be concluded?
options: Interspecific competition between A and B is proven, because A colonises and grows well in every single plot from which B was removed.
Competition is indicated but not proven, because A's success could depend on other factors that differ where B is absent.
The initial survey of where A and B occur was an experiment, so by itself it establishes that they compete.
The two species cannot be competing, because barnacles are fixed in place and were not seen to fight each other.
mcqs.specStatementText: Testing for competition: experiment or observation
mcqs.explain: One species being more successful in the absence of another indicates competition but does not prove it. The removal experiment strengthens the case by manipulating one variable, but other differences between plots, and between the two species' tolerances, are not ruled out.
rationales: A student who treats a pattern that fits the hypothesis as proof picks this. In fact the guide states that greater success in the absence of another species indicates but does not prove competition.

One species being more successful in the absence of another indicates competition but does not prove it. The removal experiment strengthens the case by manipulating one variable, but other differences between plots, and between the two species' tolerances, are not ruled out.
A student who calls any planned data collection an experiment picks this. In fact the survey was an observation, because nothing was manipulated; only the scraping of B from plots was an experiment.
A student who thinks competition needs a contest picks this. In fact sessile organisms compete by occupying space and taking resources; no contact or fighting is required.

mcqs.q: Ecologists want to test the hypothesis that two limpet species compete for algae on a shore. Which approach tests the hypothesis by experiment rather than by observation?
options: Recording the abundance of both limpet species in quadrats placed at random positions along the shore.
Measuring the shell sizes of both limpet species in laboratory tanks of seawater collected from the shore.
Removing one limpet species from marked plots and recording the growth of the other over a year.
Comparing where each limpet species occurred in shore surveys made over the past twenty years.
mcqs.specStatementText: Testing for competition: experiment or observation
mcqs.explain: An experiment deliberately changes a variable and records the effect. Field manipulation by removal of one species is one of the experimental approaches the guide names; the untouched plots act as the control.
rationales: A student who thinks planned data collection makes an experiment picks this. In fact random sampling records what is already there without altering it, so it is a field observation.
A student who uses the laboratory as the cue for 'experiment' picks this. In fact nothing is manipulated; measuring the limpets indoors is still an observation.

An experiment deliberately changes a variable and records the effect. Field manipulation by removal of one species is one of the experimental approaches the guide names; the untouched plots act as the control.
A student who equates careful analysis of data with experimentation picks this. In fact survey records are observations; hypotheses can be tested with them, but no variable was changed.

mcqs.q: Fur records from the Hudson's Bay Company show snowshoe hare and Canada lynx numbers rising and falling in cycles of about ten years, with each peak in lynx numbers occurring one to two years after a peak in hares. Which explanation is correct?
options: Abundant hares let more lynx survive and breed, so lynx rise later; more lynx then reduce hares, after which lynx decline and hares recover.
Lynx and hare numbers should peak at the same time, so the delay of one to two years shows that the fur records were unreliable.
The lynx eat nearly all the hares, so each crash is followed by a period with no lynx at all until new ones immigrate into the area.
Predation is density-independent, so the cycles must instead be driven by alternating runs of harsh winters and milder winters.
mcqs.specStatementText: Predator and prey numbers cycle, with the predator lagging
mcqs.explain: This is density-dependent control in both directions: predation intensifies as hares become dense, and the predator population is itself limited by prey. The delay arises because lynx take time to breed in response to food and time to starve when it is scarce.
rationales: This is density-dependent control in both directions: predation intensifies as hares become dense, and the predator population is itself limited by prey. The delay arises because lynx take time to breed in response to food and time to starve when it is scarce.
A student who expects an immediate response picks this. In fact the lag is the expected signature of a predator–prey cycle, because predator reproduction responds to prey abundance with a delay.
A student who pictures predators as unstoppable picks this. In fact lynx starve and breed less as hares become scarce, so their numbers fall before the hares are eliminated and the cycle continues.

A student who thinks only competition is density-dependent picks this. In fact the risk of predation increases with prey density, and the predator–prey relationship is the guide's example of density-dependent control.

mcqs.q: After sea otters were hunted almost to extinction along parts of the North Pacific coast, sea urchin numbers increased greatly and the kelp forests were grazed away. Which statement about population control in this community is correct?
options: Neither type of control is shown, because otters do not eat kelp and so their loss cannot have affected it.
Top-down control is dominant: the predator limited the herbivore, which in turn limited the producer below it.
Top-down control is shown, which demonstrates that nutrient supply plays no part in limiting this community.
Bottom-up control is dominant, because the effect of losing the otters travelled down to the kelp at the base of the food chain.
mcqs.specStatementText: Control can come from the top or the bottom
mcqs.explain: Control originating from a higher trophic level and acting on the levels below is top-down. Otters limited urchins, which limited kelp; removing the otters released both lower levels in turn. Bottom-up control by nutrient supply still operates but is not dominant here.
rationales: A student who considers only direct feeding links picks this. In fact the effect passed along the food chain: fewer otters meant more urchins, and more urchins meant less kelp.

Control originating from a higher trophic level and acting on the levels below is top-down. Otters limited urchins, which limited kelp; removing the otters released both lower levels in turn. Bottom-up control by nutrient supply still operates but is not dominant here.

A student who treats the two types of control as mutually exclusive picks this. In fact both are possible in any community; the evidence shows that top-down control is dominant, not that bottom-up control is absent.
A student who names the control by where the effect ends up picks this. In fact the terms refer to where control originates: here a predator at the top drove the changes, so control is top-down.

mcqs.q: In what way are allelopathy in plants and the secretion of antibiotics by microorganisms similar?
options: In both, a chemical is released to destroy pathogens that would otherwise cause disease in the producer.
In both, a chemical is released as a defence against the animals that would otherwise eat the producer.
In both, a chemical substance is released into the surroundings to deter potential competitors.
In both, the producer must make direct contact with a competitor before the chemical acts.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chemical warfare against competitors
mcqs.explain: Allelopathic plants such as black walnut release chemicals that inhibit neighbouring plants, and microorganisms such as Penicillium secrete antibiotics that inhibit competing bacteria. In each case the chemical reduces competition for limited resources.
rationales: A student who knows antibiotics only as medicines picks this. In fact the antibiotic targets microorganisms competing for the same resources, and allelopathic chemicals target competing plants, not pathogens.

A student who assumes every plant toxin is aimed at herbivores picks this. In fact allelopathy acts on other plants that compete for light, water and mineral ions, and antibiotics act on other microorganisms.

Allelopathic plants such as black walnut release chemicals that inhibit neighbouring plants, and microorganisms such as Penicillium secrete antibiotics that inhibit competing bacteria. In each case the chemical reduces competition for limited resources.
A student who thinks competition requires a confrontation picks this. In fact the chemical diffuses into the soil or the surrounding medium and acts on competitors that the producer never touches.

mcqs.q: Very few plants grow beneath a black walnut tree, and bacteria fail to grow close to a colony of Penicillium mould on a piece of bread. Which option correctly names the two processes?
options: Defence against herbivores by the walnut; antibiotic secretion by the mould.
Allelopathy by the walnut; treatment of the bread's bacterial disease by the mould.
Pathogenicity by the walnut towards plants; pathogenicity by the mould towards bacteria.
Allelopathy by the walnut tree; secretion of an antibiotic by the mould.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chemical warfare against competitors
mcqs.explain: Black walnut releases juglone into the soil, which inhibits the growth of competing plants beneath it, an example of allelopathy. Penicillium secretes penicillin, which prevents bacteria from growing on the same food source, an example of antibiotic secretion.
rationales: A student who assumes plant chemicals target animals picks this. In fact juglone suppresses other plants competing with the walnut for resources; it is not a defence against being eaten.
A student who thinks of antibiotics as cures picks this. In fact the mould secretes penicillin to deter bacteria competing for the bread, the same competitive purpose as allelopathy.

A student who uses 'pathogen' for anything that harms picks this. In fact pathogenicity is disease caused by a microorganism or virus living in a host; neither the walnut nor the mould lives inside the organisms it inhibits.

Black walnut releases juglone into the soil, which inhibits the growth of competing plants beneath it, an example of allelopathy. Penicillium secretes penicillin, which prevents bacteria from growing on the same food source, an example of antibiotic secretion.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes the exchange between an orchid and its mycorrhizal fungus?
options: The fungus supplies mineral ions and, to the seedling, carbon compounds; the photosynthesizing orchid supplies sugars.
The fungus fixes nitrogen gas into ammonia for the orchid; the orchid supplies the fungus with sugars made in photosynthesis.
The fungus takes sugars from the orchid's roots and the orchid gains nothing in return, so the fungus is really a parasite.
The fungus supplies the orchid with mineral ions and water but receives nothing in return from the orchid.
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutualism: both partners gain
mcqs.explain: Orchid seeds are minute and have almost no food reserves, so the seedling depends on the fungus for carbon compounds as well as water and mineral ions absorbed by the hyphae. Once the orchid has leaves it supplies sugars to the fungus, so both partners benefit.
rationales: Orchid seeds are minute and have almost no food reserves, so the seedling depends on the fungus for carbon compounds as well as water and mineral ions absorbed by the hyphae. Once the orchid has leaves it supplies sugars to the fungus, so both partners benefit.

A student who merges mycorrhizae with root nodules picks this. In fact nitrogen fixation is carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium; mycorrhizal fungi absorb mineral ions that are already in the soil.

A student who assumes a fungus inside roots must be an infection picks this. In fact orchid seeds cannot germinate without the fungus, which supplies the seedling with the carbon compounds and mineral ions it lacks.
A student who remembers only the plant's benefit picks this. In fact mutualism requires both to benefit: the fungus receives sugars from the orchid once the orchid photosynthesizes.

mcqs.q: Two lichen species were recorded as present or absent in 80 random quadrats on a stone wall: both present 16, only A present 32, only B present 24, neither 8. If the two species were distributed independently of each other, how many quadrats would be expected to contain both species?
options: 16 quadrats
24 quadrats
20 quadrats
30 quadrats
mcqs.specStatementText: Chi-squared for association between two species
mcqs.explain: Species A is present in 16 + 32 = 48 quadrats and species B in 16 + 24 = 40. Expected frequency = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total = 48 × 40 ÷ 80 = 24. Both species were observed together in only 16 quadrats, fewer than expected, so the association is negative.
rationales: A student who does not separate the observed count from the expected value, and reads the number of quadrats that actually contain both species as the answer, picks this. In fact 16 is the observed frequency; the expected frequency under independence is 48 × 40 ÷ 80 = 24, and the test compares the two.

Species A is present in 16 + 32 = 48 quadrats and species B in 16 + 24 = 40. Expected frequency = (row total × column total) ÷ grand total = 48 × 40 ÷ 80 = 24. Both species were observed together in only 16 quadrats, fewer than expected, so the association is negative.

A student who assumes that independence makes the four combinations equally likely divides 80 by 4 and picks this. In fact the expected values depend on how common each species is: A occurs in 60% of quadrats and B in 50%, so both are expected in 0.6 × 0.5 × 80 = 24.

A student who multiplies the two percentages (60% of quadrats contain A, 50% contain B) and reports the resulting 30% as if it were a number of quadrats picks this. In fact 30% is the expected fraction; 30% of the 80 quadrats is 24.

mcqs.q: Why does competition occur between members of the same population?
options: It does not occur: members of one species share their resources, and competition arises only between different species.
It occurs only when two individuals confront each other over the same item of food, the same mate or the same nesting site.
Individuals of one species have identical needs, so when a resource is scarce what one uses leaves less for others.
It occurs only in solitary species, because individuals living together in a group are by definition cooperating.
mcqs.specStatementText: Same species: compete and cooperate
mcqs.explain: Members of a population need exactly the same food, water, light, space, mates or nest sites. Whenever such a resource is in limited supply, each individual's consumption reduces the amount available to the rest, which is why intraspecific competition arises.
rationales: A student whose picture of one species is a herd or flock picks this. In fact intraspecific competition is often the most intense competition of all: trees in a stand compete for light and male red deer compete for mates, precisely because they need the same things.

A student who thinks competition means a contest picks this. In fact competition occurs whenever a limited resource is shared: seedlings shading one another and animals feeding from the same depleted food supply compete without any confrontation.

Members of a population need exactly the same food, water, light, space, mates or nest sites. Whenever such a resource is in limited supply, each individual's consumption reduces the amount available to the rest, which is why intraspecific competition arises.

A student who equates grouping with cooperation picks this. In fact members of a grazing herd or a nesting colony still compete for grass, mates and nest sites; cooperation and competition can both occur within the same group.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic C4.1 Populations and communities

Estimate by random sampling, and accept sampling error
Quadrats for things that stay put
Mark, release, recapture for things that move
Carrying capacity is set by limited resources
Density-dependent factors push numbers back towards carrying capacity
The sigmoid curve is a model, and real populations can overshoot it
Growing a population in the lab
A community is all the living things in an ecosystem
Invasive species win the competition for resources
Testing for competition: experiment or observation
Chi-squared for association between two species
Predator and prey numbers cycle, with the predator lagging
Control can come from the top or the bottom

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No concept, misconception or item asks students to recall or apply the formula for standard deviation, and no item requires a standard deviation to be calculated by hand. Standard deviation appears only as a value already given, to be interpreted as a measure of how evenly a population is spread between quadrats.

Carrying capacity is defined simply as the maximum population size of a species that an environment can support sustainably, with named limiting resources (food, water, light, space, mineral nutrients, nesting sites). No logistic equation, r and K notation, or numerical modelling of carrying capacity is included.

The sigmoid population growth curve is described throughout as an exponential phase, a transitional phase and a plateau phase only. No lag phase is named in any concept, misconception or item, and no item treats a lag phase as a required part of the model.

omitted.sequence: no authored ordering; would require inventing a sequence
